newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech Republic grapples with new advertising era.
newsitem.headline: Czech Republic grapples with new advertising era.

text.p: Czechoslovakia's Velvet Revolution in 1989 gave birth to new freedoms at all levels, but also to problems -- unleashing an advertising industry on consumers and legislators ill-prepared to deal with commercials.
"Six, seven years ago this was a country without a single billboard," Vladimir Zelezny, director-general of the Czech Republic's TV NOVA television network, told a conference in Prague on Wednesday.

"You would switch on your TV and see an advertisement for bridge construction. Now it is a country that is one of the most important for advertising," Zelezny told the "West Goes East" conference on advertising and self-regulation in Eastern and Central Europe.
The strict censorship imposed under communist rule has given way to a virtual free-for-all compared to the strict policies under which advetisers operate in Western Europe.
Billboards promoting the "Great American Taste" of Phillip Morris cigarettes line the road from the Prague airport to the city centre.
One foreign journalist based in Prague said strict censorship of communism has given way to a raft of adverts ranging from the overtly sexual to simple poor taste.

Jan Kasal, vice president of the Czech House of Representatives, cited to the conference two billboard adverts highlighting questions of taste: one featuring dog excrement and another showing a naked Adam, with a mobile phone instead of a fig leaf covering his genitals.
The Czech Republic was the first former Soviet bloc country to adopt a Western-style self-regulating system for advertising.
But it continues to struggle over when the industry should be left to regulate itself and when the government should step in.
"We do not have 200 members of Parliament who have a deep understanding of what advertising is," said Kasal. "But we have 200 legislators who want to get this understanding."
TV NOVA's Zelezny said much of the regulatory confusion reflects how legislators drew from a hodge-podge of Western laws rather than developing laws tailored to the Czech Republic.
"Our legislation has been cannibalised," he said, likening the process to trying to build new cars using parts scavenged from old cars.
The lack of a cohesive policy has led to problems for private broadcasters like TV NOVA, which began broadcasting in 1994.

"Our first year of broadcasting was a battle with the legislation," Kasal said. Broadcasters continue to fight with legislators over interpretation of laws, including whether non-prescription drugs can be advertised on television and during which programmes.
At the same time, Eastern European countries are staggering under the growing influence from the West on advertising and consumer habits.

Martin Tod, marketing director for Procter & Gamble in the Czech Repubic, said the consumer products company -- the world's largest advertiser -- used advertising to introduce its products to new consumers in Eastern Europe.
Western products are finding an increasingly large market in Eastern Europe, where buying Western goods is a way of showing off new-found affluence and sophistication.
The pattern has been well demonstrated in the sale of alcoholic beverages.

"Always in a growing economy there is the aspiration toward imported brands," Henry Pomeroy, director of corporate affairs for Allied Domecq, told Reuters. "In this country there is a trend to scotch whisky and gin versus white spirits and beers."

Public opinion surveys in the Czech Republic have shown a consumer distaste for some Western attitudes toward advertising, said Jiri Mikes, an executive with the Czech advertising self- regulating body, Rada Pro Reklamu.
"In some situations foreign companies do here what they are not allowed to do at home," said Petr Hajn, chairman of Rada Pro Reklamu, the Czech advertising industry's self-regulating body.
